webTitle: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers

fields.headline: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
fields.trailText: Act divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US allies
fields.bodyText: The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago. The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results. However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead. The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports. It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions. Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill. Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”. “Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries. The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members. “I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday. “I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.” The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote. “We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

webTitle: Morning Mail: AI tipping point warning; concerns about aged care scheme; and a US rate hike

fields.headline: Morning Mail: AI tipping point warning; concerns about aged care scheme; and a US rate hike
fields.trailText: Tech godfather Yoshua Bengio is ‘optimistic’ about action on AI because the ‘public is moving’; US Fed defies Trump to raise borrowing costs
fields.bodyText: Morning everyone. One of the godfathers of AI technology has warned that we are fast-approaching a Covid-style inflection point where governments have to act to protect the public. We also report on JD Vance shrugging off calls for regulation and have an explainer on what proposals to allow an AI scrape of Australian content means. Federal health officials were left in turmoil by an algorithm to determine aged care packages, Guardian analysis reveals how the grants program massively favoured Labor, US rates go up for the first time since 2023, and what’s behind the explosion in new Asian fast-food chains? Australia Granted | Federal Labor seats have received more than 90% of funds already awarded in the first five months of a controversial multimillion-dollar grants program, Guardian Australia analysis reveals, adding to concerns over the scheme’s selection process. Aged care turmoil | Federal health officials were in turmoil before the rollout of an algorithm to determine funding packages for older Australians after discovering legislation had been drafted so rigidly that the tool could not legally be overridden by aged care assessors. Land fear | Local Aboriginal land councils in New South Wales say they remain deeply concerned about changes to laws governing crown land that could retrospectively affect land claims. Migration shift | Foreign students are set to face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia as the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, prepares to outline the government’s immigration reforms at the National Press Club in Canberra today. Emergency measure | A new institute dedicated to improving emergency medical care for severely injured children will be established in New South Wales after recent high-profile trauma events in the state. World Rate hike | The US Federal Reserve has voted to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023 as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation. Follow it live. AI tipping point | Concerns over AI safety are reaching a point where governments realise they must act to protect the public, similarly to the Covid pandemic, according to one of the “godfathers” of the technology. The US vice-president, JD Vance, has dismissed calls for global regulation of AI safety risks, telling companies: “If you’re building Frankenstein, stop.” The US House speaker called an early recess before the midterms, thwarting hopes for progress on regulation. The boom in datacentres such as the one announced for Queensland yesterday will create a “tsunami” of discarded electronics and toxic e-waste, a new report projects. NAZA threats | Threats by the Israeli military, ministers and far-right activists have intensified against the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of NAZA, a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. It has been confirmed that the US has decided not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back a Houthi advance inside Yemen. The Hague | Hashim Thaçi, the former president of Kosovo, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a tribunal in The Hague for war crimes, including dozens of murders committed in Kosovo’s war against Serbia. US immigration | The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that the country’s majority black government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners. Full Story The ‘apex predator’ of fires choking south-east Asia Europe’s catastrophic summer made headlines in Australia, but wildfires in Indonesia have received little coverage. Matilda Boseley discusses the crisis with Kate Lamb. In-depth The possibility that AI companies could get unrestricted access to everything Australians create online has led to privacy concerns. We look at what the government proposals mean for you, how they might affect access, and whether tech firms will invest here as a result. Our data guru argues that the dominance of AI is not inevitable and that countries could act together to regulate its impact. Not the news With bright, cheery and cutesy marketing aimed at young people, a slew of Asian fast-food chains are making their mark on our streets. Isabella Lee talks to diners about the appeal of eateries such as Marrybrown (Malaysian halal fried chicken), Nana’s Green Tea (a Japanese cafe brand) and Molly Tea (premium Chinese bubble tea). Sport Formula One | Formula One has announced its calendar for 2027, with an increase in sprint races to 10 events, including at Melbourne which will be the third grand prix of the year on 4 April. AFL | Hawthorn take on the champions, Brisbane Lions, in the second of the two preliminary finals in Melbourne tomorrow night. Will it be a changing of the guard? Martin Pegan runs the rule over the two sides. Football | There’s Europa League action this morning that you can follow live here, plus more Carabao Cup action including Manchester United at home to Brighton. Media roundup Kevin Parker, the frontman of Tame Impala and Dockers fan, has reignited controversy about the club’s sponsorship by Woodside, WAtoday reports. The Herald Sun thinks it knows who will replace Karl Stefanovic and Sarah Abo on the Today show. People living near Adelaide’s Northfield pre-release centre say they are petrified about the release of Snowtown killer James Vlassakis, the Advertiser reports. The Ballarat Courier asks whether politicians are doing enough to fix potholes after the death of a motorcyclist on Sunday. What’s happening today Education | National student strike in protest at Pauline Hanson and One Nation. Technology | Parliamentary AI industry showcase in Canberra from 9.30am with Andrew Charlton, Victor Dominello, Melissa Price and Sally Sitou. Defence | Australia’s ambassador to the US is speaking at an Aukus event in Washington DC. webTitle: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel

fields.headline: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel
fields.trailText: Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs
fields.bodyText: The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of the largest US arms transfers of Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel. Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal. “The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.” The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads. Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April. In 2025, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, declared a national security emergency to bypass congressional review and fast-track nearly $3bn in weapons, including more than 35,000 heavy bombs and 4,000 bunker-buster warheads. With a separate $6.67bn package in January, the administration has now cleared or expedited over $12bn in arms for Israel since Trump took office. Meeks has said the pace has outrun oversight, accusing officials of skipping briefings and rushing sales while raising alarms over Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. The hold also lands amid longstanding accusations that Israel has used American weapons unlawfully. The Leahy laws bar US assistance to foreign military units credibly linked to extrajudicial killings and serious abuse; the state department in 2024 flagged at least five Israeli units on those grounds before the war in Gaza even began, including one battalion tied to the death of a Palestinian American at a West Bank checkpoint. The Geneva conventions, meanwhile, bar arming a party where there is a clear risk of war crimes – a standard a UN commission of inquiry cited last year in finding Israel’s Gaza campaign amounted to genocide and calling on the US and other states to halt weapons transfers. In 2024, Biden administration lawyers, including some at the state department, had concluded it was reasonable to assess that Israel had violated international humanitarian law and Leahy laws by using American weapons in Gaza, even as the administration publicly avoided making that determination. Meeks, long known for his strong pro-Israel views, emphasized that the hold was not a break with the country itself. “This decision does not diminish congressional support for Israel’s legitimate defense needs,” he said. “It reflects Congress’s responsibility to ensure that US-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly and with meaningful safeguards for human life.” The state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

webTitle: ‘Inflation is too high and has been for too long,’ says Kevin Warsh as Fed announces rate hikes – as it happened

fields.headline: ‘Inflation is too high and has been for too long,’ says Kevin Warsh as Fed announces rate hikes – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: The US Federal Reserve voted unanimously to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, in a decision that marks chair Kevin Warsh’s first major step to try to tamp down inflation. The Fed’s open market committee voted 12-0 to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a new range of 3.75% to 4%, potentially setting Warsh on a collision course with Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed for rates to be cut and nominated Warsh with that expectation. Warsh, who assumed the role in May, said the Fed had concluded that “the plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Although Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war against Iran by name. He also declined to provide an indication of whether or not this hike will be the first in a series of increases, as has typically happened in the past. Warsh also declined to comment on Trump’s demands and threats and how he might react, asserting that Fed’s independence means: “We stay in our lane.” We’ve yet to hear from Donald Trump on what he makes of the news, but no doubt we will soon. In the meantime, here’s our report: Major US indexes turned lower as Kevin Warsh’s comments came to an end earlier, with the S&P 500 down 0.9%, the Dow tumbling by 850 points and the Nasdaq down 0.5%. Meanwhile, US treasury securities were mixed. The 2-year yield, most sensitive to expectations for future Fed policy, rose six basis points to 4.725% after earlier declining. The 10-year yield was up one basis point at 5% and the 30-year yield was down 1.6 basis points at 5.347%. And the US dollar index rose 0.6% to 100.25. Business editor Donald Trump has still yet to speak but at least one Republican has come out against the Fed’s decision. “With the economy growing, businesses hiring and investing, and inflation at less than half the rate American families endured under President Biden, interest rates should be coming down, not going up,” the representative Jason Smith of Missouri, who leads the top tax committee in the House, said in a statement. “American workers, families, and small businesses have waited long enough for relief from high borrowing costs that make it harder to buy a home, start a business, or get ahead. This is the wrong decision for working families that will only prolong the high costs they are paying.” And further to his statement, which we brought you earlier, Democrat Brendan Boyle, the ranking member on the House budget committee, says on X: The Federal Reserve just raised interest rates because Donald Trump’s tariff taxes and Iran war have sent inflation soaring. It’s been over two years since Trump promised to lower costs on ‘Day One.’ Instead, he’s done the exact opposite. Today’s decision to raise interest rates was “inevitable”, says Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, “with energy prices taking a renewed step higher and inflation remaining persistently well above target”. He added: This is a pivotal moment for Kevin Warsh too. He was brought into the Fed as Trump’s guy, poised to deliver the rate cuts he so desperately wants. However, his first move of significant impact is in fact an interest rate rise, and this risks hampering the relationship between the two and thus a repeat of the barbs Jerome Powell suffered during his tenure. Warsh will be hoping this action is swift, although energy prices are ultimately what is driving inflation right now rather than what is going on within the US economy. In a note to investors, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said: The Fed appears to be on board with our view that its hike today will be followed by one more later this year. While the latest Summary of Economic Projections implies that the Fed may be content with just two hikes in total, we judge that Fed officials are underestimating the potential for the unemployment rate to decline, meaning we are sticking with our forecast for a third hike in early 2027 as well. “I love the inflation,” Donald Trump infamously said back in June, arguing that price rises were just temporary and would drop sharply once his war on Iran was concluded. But the war continues and so do high gas prices. Warsh earlier made the case that prices are too high: “The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long. This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have a meaningfully improved.” Warsh stresses that the central bank’s decision to raise interest rates was not influenced by financial markets. We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation. I’ll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision. Taking questions from reporters, Warsh has declined to comment on Donald Trump’s repeated calls for rates to be cut, not raised. “I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president,” he replied to one reporter. Later, when another reporter brought up Trump’s threats to cut off trade with certain countries, and asked Warsh when he last spoke to the US president, if he anticipates a post-decision meeting and if this is another test to the Fed’s independence, he reiterated: You gave me a long menu from which to choose, they’re all very tempting. I don’t have anything for you on discussions with the president. And I am not a Wall Street newsletter. Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street. We will let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane. That is the way we can stand up here and call them the way we see them. Warsh adds of the rate hike: “Those who are least well off have the most to gain from a durable expansion, a solid labor market and stable prices.” “At our July meeting, we all agreed that inflation remained too high, and we expressed our joint readiness to act as circumstances might require,” Warsh says. “And a good majority of my colleagues and I thought the wiser course then would be to weight new information in the inter-meeting period. “In the last month in Wyoming, I expressed my commitment to a monetary policy discipline, not to a decision. I defined the standard for action. We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. “Today the FOMC decide that this standard has not been satisfied.” Yet, for more than five years, inflation has been running above target, Warsh goes on, so the Fed’s predominant focus is on the price stability side of its mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long. He adds: “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” “One basic sign of strength is the state of America’s labour markets,” Warsh says, highlighting the low unemployment rate, rising weekly hours and the relatively low rate at which people are filing for unemployment benefits. The labour side of the Fed’s congressional agreement is in good shape. “Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening,” Warsh says. Citing consumer spending, capital investment and other indicators, he adds: Consider the geopolitical landscape of shocks and uncertainty, and you begin to appreciate the resilience of the US economy. Kevin Warsh is speaking now. He starts off by reiterating what the committee released in its press statement. I’ll bring you all the key lines here. Democratic congressman Brendan Boyle, who is the ranking member of the House budget committee, released this statement reacting to the news: Today’s rate hike is further proof that Donald Trump and Republicans have failed on the economy. When Trump took office, inflation was falling. But just today, diesel hit the highest price on record. Trump’s reckless tariffs and disastrous war in Iran have sent prices soaring again, leading to the Federal Reserve decision to raise rates. Donald Trump will undoubtedly try to blame anyone but himself for this rate hike. But if he wants to know who caused it, he should look in the mirror. Kay Haigh, global head and CIO of Fixed Income and Liquidity Solutions at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, has this analysis of today’s decision: The Fed has signalled it does not at this stage envisage an aggressive tightening cycle. Most FOMC members see a total of two hikes this year per the SEP, and it will likely skip October’s meeting given its proximity to the midterm elections. One more hike this year in December is our base case, although this remains contingent on upcoming CPI reports and the path of energy prices. Business editor The 12-0 decision will be a blow to Donald Trump, who wanted Kevin Warsh to cut rates. The vote means two other Trump Fed appointees – Michelle Bowman and Christopher Waller – agreed that it was time to raise rates, undercutting any potential messaging from the White House that Warsh and co had been pressured into a rate hike by the other members of the Federal Open Market Committee. The ongoing US-Israel war against Iran has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31. Concerns about inflation have induced a sell-off in the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market can lead to higher interest rates for consumer and business loans. The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates affect mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering them in 2024 and 2025. At the beginning of the year, when the annualised inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in August remained stubbornly high while unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike. Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased. Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according to recent Pew Research Center data. Meanwhile, Donald Trump has implored Republican voters to pretend as if they are voting for him on their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress. Critics have called the move akin to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached a record-high $40tn last month. Here’s Gaya’s report: We’ve yet to hear from the White House and Donald Trump hasn’t been active on his Truth Social platform so far today, but we’ll no doubt get his reaction to the news soon. The rate increase is a turnaround for the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh – who we’ll hear from shortly – and sets him up for a potential showdown with Donald Trump, who nominated him for the job. Warsh had often suggested last year when under consideration by the US president that the Fed could reduce its key rate, echoing the president’s call for lower borrowing costs. But Trump’s war on Iran has evidently changed all that, and Warsh has emphasised several times since taking over the role in May that he was committed to the Fed’s independence from political pressures. The decision was unanimous, with the vote 12–0. In its press release, the committee said: Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability. Business editor As expected, the committee said it has “decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.75-4%, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate. The committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.” According to a Duke University survey of 32 former Fed governors, regional presidents and staffers, 29 endorsed a rate hike, two didn’t respond and one said the Fed should hold rates steady. “The Fed and new chair’s credibility is on the line,” one former official said. Another participant said: I am no longer confident that PCE inflation will return to 2% in the next year or two without the Fed raising interest rates. Above all, the upside risks to the inflation outlook have worsened since July: energy prices have not reversed as expected, tariff pass-through continues, and the AI build-out is adding to price pressures. Another person said: Earlier in the year, it appeared that there was some hope that inflation would decline closer to its 2 percent target within a year or two. That now appears less likely. While some of the effects of tariffs and war-induced shortages may manifest as price-level effects, with temporary inflation consequences, it’s hard to have much confidence in that. Thus, a more sustained increase in inflation is quite possible. Clearly, none of those who responded to the poll backed a rate cut, which Donald Trump has been pushing for. However, they also didn’t think dramatically high rate increases would be necessary to tackle the inflation challenge. Business editor The Fed has two mandates: price stability and supporting the job market. The jobs market has remained robust but spikes in energy prices have put the central bank under pressure to raise rates in order to bring down inflation. Americans have spent over $100bn extra on gasoline and diesel during Trump’s war on Iran than they would have had there been no war, according to estimates by the Climate Solutions Lab at Brown University. Good afternoon. The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023 amid persistently high inflation. After deciding to hold rates steady at its last meeting in July, the Fed is now anticipated to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point (25 basis points), bringing the benchmark federal funds rate to a new target range of 3.75% to 4%. The central bank’s last increase effectively bookended its Covid pandemic response, but inflation has remained above its 2% target for more than five years now and has been further exacerbated by Donald Trump’s disastrous and ongoing war against Iran. The US president has repeatedly demanded that rates be cut, creating intense pressure on his handpicked chair, Kevin Warsh. On Sunday, days before the Fed’s September meeting was due to kick off, Trump said the United States should have “the lowest interest rate in the world” regardless of what the data indicates about inflation or the economy. If he decides to go ahead with the hike, Warsh will no doubt infuriate the president, who regularly attacked his predecessor Jerome Powell. Trump has so far been more supportive of Warsh since he took charge earlier this year, but he’s become more vocal recently. “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” the president posted on social media two weeks ago. The Fed’s decision comes just weeks out from November’s crucial US midterm elections, which will determine whether or not Trump’s Republican party retains control of Congress, with affordability and the cost-of-living crisis the major issue for voters. The Fed is due to release its decision at 2pm ET, and Warsh will hold a press conference at 2.30. We’ll bring you all the latest here, so stay tuned.

webTitle: ‘A sense of energy’: Our politics team answered your questions on Democrats’ midterms hopes

fields.headline: ‘A sense of energy’: Our politics team answered your questions on Democrats’ midterms hopes
fields.trailText: Who are the Democrats running in the midterms, and where do they stand? Our US political reporters discussed the state of the Democrats, the party’s moderate and leftwing candidates and key races to watch
fields.bodyText: Thank you for joining us and for the thoughtful questions! We’ll be hosting these types of conversations covering a range of topics, now until the midterm elections on November 3. We’ll keep asking party leaders, elected officials and candidates these same kinds of questions as we cover this year’s midterms. And we’re all over the country this year hearing from voters like you to understand what matters to them. To keep up with our coverage of the midterms sign up to the Stakes newsletter here and bookmark our US midterm elections page. Anonymous123456 asks: Do you think that the Democrats have risen to the occasion following Trump’s historic low polling numbers, and have they truly capitalised on the growing momentum of anti-establishment sentiments, with more people feeling politically homeless and disenfranchised? Alice: I don’t think they have and one of the things I hear most often from people is how deflated they feel about their Democratic representatives. Who has seized on the anti-establishment sentiment and both anger at Trump but also deep frustration with Democrats’ timidity however are the many leftist candidates, including several young political newcomers, who have swept primary races this summer. The Democratic Socialists of America, who have backed some but not all of them, have in a way become a “shorthand” for that momentum. DSA membership has soared to 120,000 in recent months. Within a day of the New York primaries – where they won nine out of 10 races in which they fielded candidates – more than 900 people joined the NYC chapter. Of course it remains to be seen how leftist candidates across the country will fare in the midterms, and more importantly how they will navigate their new position when they get to Congress. DSA’s swift rise has not always been smooth and there are plenty of major debates happening within the organization. But I think their momentum sends a clear signal to Democrats that they have fallen far short of voters’ calls for big, bold change. Puttyinhishand asks: How will the US relationship with Israel play out for the Democrats in the campaign? Alice: I think the monumental shift in US public opinion on Israel that followed the latest war in Gaza is transforming electoral politics in ways that we’re only beginning to see. Israel played an outsize role in the New York City mayoral race last year — a municipal race for an office that has very little to do with foreign policy. Reflexive support for Israel which was once viewed as a prerequisite for political viability is not only no longer a safe bet, but increasingly an actual liability. AIPAC funding has become deeply toxic. Democrats have already been dealing with a reckoning over Israel’s plunging popularity and many of the progressive wins of this primary season are explained at least in part by that; in some races support for Israel was the only clear difference between competing progressive candidates. In New York, Darializa Avila Chevalier, a young political newcomer, scored one of the greatest upsets of the primary season with a campaign - “babies not bombs” - that was originally launched in protest of the incumbent’s positions on Israel. I think it remains to be seen how much this will play a role in the midterms – there are too many other issues on the table for any one of them to be the decisive one – but even Republicans are increasingly split on Israel, and many favor candidates prioritizing the US economy over military aid abroad. David: I don’t think it will matter as much as Trump or the economy, and it will matter in some districts more than others. Still, it’s become a divisive and potentially damaging issue for Democrats. It’s amazing how quickly public opinion has shifted: six in 10 US adults, and eight in 10 Democrats, have an unfavorable view of Israel, according to Pew Research in April. The party is moving too: in July more than a hundred House Democrats voted to slash military aid to the country, which would once have been unthinkable. The debate has turned rancorous online, especially around figures such as Hasan Piker, whom Republicans are working hard to tie to Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. That’s a state where this whole issue could blow up for Democrats. But I suspect it will come to a head in the 2028 presidential primary: every candidate will be asked if the situation in Gaza constitutes a genocide. A user on Instagram asks: Why can’t the dems win the Senate after all these years and failed policies? / With things so bad, how are the Dems not guaranteed a win? Shrai: This is really the multimillion dollar (or maybe $5,000) question. Obviously it’s all still to play for, and Democrats need to pick up four seats to reclaim the chamber. But these are key battlegrounds, and some of them are states that Trump flipped in 2024 (North Carolina and Michigan). As we’ve discussed, the anti-Trump animus is a really strong force that could propel Dems across the line in November (his approval rating is at a new low). But, despite his insistence, the president isn’t actually on the ballot, and some of the Republican nominees for Senate have, perhaps tactically, made less of a song and dance about Trump’s support. Swing voters in places like Alaska, Maine and Michigan aren’t a monolith and they’re really weighing whether the Republicans on the ballot might be able to actually do enough to curb Trump or if they take the plunge and vote for the Democrat, who might feel like a real risk in their mind. David: I get the sentiment of this question. Many political commentators have ranked Trump, twice impeached and the first convicted criminal to serve in the White House, as the worst president in US history. It’s astonishing that these elections are still potentially even close. (There are of course lots of reasons around perceived self-interest, the influence of money in politics, the rightwing media machine and Democrats’ various inadequacies.) Blueowl2677 asks: I have been greatly disappointed with the way the Dems ignore what their constituents want when it comes to choosing who is running. And then our wants and needs are ignored to keep playing this back and forth game with the GOP and they are beholden to their donors, not we the people. Why should I continue to vote Dem when none of this is discussed to do better within the party? What are they going to actually do differently and start passing actual common sense legislation to protect consumers more from the waste and destruction of our earth for the almighty dollar? Rachel: This year’s midterm primaries showcased some of the points you’re touching on – there has long been a sense that Democrats were deciding who should run and clearing the field to help them do so. But we’ve seen some of these party schisms playing out directly in these contested primaries, where insurgent candidates have challenged incumbents or anointed successors and, in some instances, won their races. I don’t know yet the extent that this will carry into other years, but I will say I have seen a sense of energy on the ground that I haven’t in cycles past because people actually feel like they’re making the choice, and their options feel more well-rounded. And we’ve seen, too, a strong backlash against money in politics – this cycle, having big money from pro-Israel groups, for instance, often backfired on a candidate and became a liability for them among voters and a key talking point for their opponents. How this translates into governing, assuming broader Dem victories this year, will be critical to harnessing the anti-establishment energy among voters to show that there are still ways to make meaningful changes to the status quo. Shrai: To Rachel’s point I’m really curious to see how the results of the midterms for Democrats ultimately create more of a reckoning for the party’s leadership. A number of candidates this cycle for both the House and Senate have been asked whether they would support Chuck Schumer or Hakeem Jeffries as leaders of their respective chambers if Dems flip Congress, and a number of the progressive candidates we’ve mentioned in this Q&A say it’s essentially time for “out with the old and in with the new” come January. There’s a real sense, with voters like yourself, that the establishment has done little to address the antipathy towards big money in politics (whether its AIPAC or other corporate donors) and what they see as mealy-mouthed promises and talking points. Earlier this year I used the Maine Senate race as kind of a case study for this. The party’s early bet on the septuagenarian Janet Mills was a clear miscalculation (she dropped out before the June primary) that ultimately led to the unvetted Graham Platner to rise and fall within months. Now, if Troy Jackson wins or loses, party leaders like Schumer will likely have to answer for their misplaced instincts. Joseph: That’s a fair fight to pick, and the party hasn’t won it yet. There’s a real insurgency… El-Sayed running against millions on millions of corporate money, Mamdani forcing leadership to back a nominee they didn’t want, and close to 30 more progressive primary wins behind them, from Melat Kiros unseating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado, similar to Justice Dems backed Donavan McKinney in Michigan. But the people who actually run the DNC and decide who gets funded are still the same donor-class operators who’ve stalled real cost of living and climate fights for a decade, and still are resistant to budging on Israel and Palestine. Nobody’s owed your vote. Watch what they fund, not what they say, and remember that you don’t owe anyone your loyalty. But don’t just walk away either: keep pushing the insurgents, back candidates willing to buck the party line, or if nobody’s speaking for you, consider running yourself. And if you back more moderate candidates, give them your support too. That’s how the party actually reflects the people! Citizen_Squared writes: After the disaster of the Trump years, the Democrats still do not have a clear message/vision/plan for ending the destruction Maga has done. Talking endlessly about affordability is not a governing vision. The polls may have the Democrats ahead for the House and Senate but thanks to extreme gerrymandering, voter restrictions and a big assist from the corrupt Supreme Court in striking out the Voting Rights Act, don’t be surprised if the gains by the Democrats are limited on election day. If that happens, the party will collapse into civil war. David: Yes, if Democrats underperform, there are sure to be recriminations and huge pressure on Senate leader Chuck Schumer and House leader Hakeem Jeffries (it’s been notable how many candidates are unwilling to endorse Schumer). But the day after the midterms will also fire the starting gun for the 2028 presidential primary, which will probably galvanising and energising. Candidates will come forward with their visions and that will take up a lot of oxygen. DashAkol asks: Following the 2018 midterms, we saw the Democratic theory of the case crystallize, generally tracking the 2026 Sanders campaign: voters will choose the Democratic party with a bold progressive agenda. (This didn’t carry through to Biden but captured the imaginations of many voters and of many 2020 campaign platforms more or less.) Now, following the 2026 midterms, what do we foresee as the new Democratic theory of the case? Shrai: For Democrats, these midterms live in the wake of Kamala Harris’s loss in 2024. The party is still undergoing an identity crisis which these races seem to highlight. We’re seeing battleground states choose insurgent nominees who really buck the party’s establishment (see Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Troy Jackson in Maine, Angie Nixon in Florida and several other progressives in House races in New York and Colorado). But there is also a sense that this wave isn’t applicable across the board, particularly in states where we have Democrats running on more centrist platforms (see Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire and James Talarico in Texas). If progressive candidates aren’t successful in November it could be the cudgel that the establishment uses to advocate for moderate candidates (particularly looking ahead to 2028). If they win, however, it could be the exact proof-of-concept for the party’s direction forward, and running politicians who are pushing for ideas that might have once been considered radical (thinking about Medicare for All and higher taxes on the ultra-wealthy). David: Affordability worked for both moderate and progressive Democrats in last year’s elections in New Jersey, New York and Virginia. I have to believe some flavor of that will be central in 2028: an understanding that the elites and the system have failed, that voters are struggling to make ends meet, that they fear their children will be worse off than they are. We’ve gone from an age of aspiration to an age of anxiety. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia has been good at tying this to Trump and “the Epstein class”. But how will Democrats fix it? It will also be fascinating to see how Democrats handle the issues of AI/datacenters and Israel. Eonphyre asks: Will the pervasive indoctrination against “socialist ideas” cease? Especially considering that so much considered “basic human rights and needs” is now called “leftist/socialist/communist” by this hate-mongering administration. Alice: I’m not sure the labels and name-calling will stop – Republicans have responded to the recent wave of leftist candidates’ wins with apocalyptic warnings like “the commie caucus is coming to Congress”. Republicans – joined by eight Democrats – have even adopted a resolution condemning “socialism” and specifically naming the DSA. What’s fundamentally changed is how effective that kind of language is. Growing sections of the US electorate are responding to the “Red Scare” rhetoric with essentially a shrug. A recent poll pointed to as many as one third of Democrats openly identifying as “socialist”, a term which not too long ago was viewed as a slur. Still, some candidates, particularly in swing states like Michigan and Florida, are making an effort to distance themselves from the labels and try to shift attention onto the issues. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan stressed he’s “not a socialist”, Angie Nixon in Florida said she’s a “more of a social democrat”. It’s harder to attack calls for tangible things like universal healthcare, affordability, and labor rights than to scaremonger about an ideology. David: It’s the obvious political play for Republicans. They don’t have many accomplishments of their own to brag about. Trump’s approval rating is at a historic low amid anger over rising prices and the Iran war. So their best bet is to switch the midterms from a referendum on Trump (even though he said to pretend he’s on the ballot!) to a choice, contrasting with the opposition. That’s where the fear mongering comes in. Will it work? No, not with millions of people. But maybe it will have some impact with older Fox News viewers, Latino voters with recent experience of communist regimes and other people who buy the Republican message that the so-called “communists” are “godless”. It was notable at last week’s Republican midterm convention how the red scare was tied to threats to Christianity and the notion that this red menace is being imported from abroad. Senator Ted Cruz explicitly tied communism to Islamism. DJE123 asks: The Democrats will have a long and challenging agenda if they win the House and/or the Senate. Where do they begin? Do they agree on priorities? What can they accomplish in the remaining two years of Trump’s term? Shrai: There are a number of hurdles facing Dems even if they do reclaim control of both chambers. First, they won’t have 60 votes in the Senate, so for key pieces of legislation that they’d want to pass they’ll still be subject to the filibuster, and as we’ve seen time and time again it’s hard to get Republicans to cross party lines to help pass bills. But one of the areas they’re certainly keen to double down on is investigations into the White House and many of Trump’s policies (from the ballroom project to alleged financial crimes to more oversight into the handling of the Epstein files). As David noted earlier though, just trying to be a check on the president isn’t enough though. They need to outline their key priorities if they are to control Congress, with a legislative agenda that actually pushes forward plans for bringing down costs across the board or reining in the administration when it comes to its ongoing immigration crackdown. If Dems are in control, the one thing they will certainly be able to push back on is the power of the purse — which Trump has tried to test with Republicans in power. Puttyinhishand asks: Will the “campaign/vote blue regardless of the candidate” mantra – which the Democrat left has been bludgeoned with for years – be actively honoured by the DNC and other party centrists if DSA candidates have won primaries? Rachel: So far, we have largely seen Democratic officials band together after primaries when a progressive or DSA candidate won. In Michigan, for instance, nearly all of the Democrats quickly endorsed Abdul El-Sayed. Most voters are not strongly ideological. When I’ve talked to political scientists and pollsters, they often will note that these debates over internal party labelling are high level, and that most voters don’t really care if a Democrat is a progressive, DSA, moderate in a general election. Where we’ve seen the most detraction from a sense of moderates embracing the left is from the pundit and consultant class, and I don’t know if that’s all that influential on voter behavior – though it certainly takes up a lot of media airtime. SF1964PA asks: Why can’t the established, relatively conservative wing of the party (Schumer, Jeffries, etc) see the value of the left-leaning younger members, and welcome them? Build out the party like the right did with the Tea Party. Rachel: They have a reflexive understanding of what they think will win the most seats for Democrats, and it’s running to the center. I’d argue this is outdated and out of step from what I hear from voters across the political spectrum, who are largely just pissed at everyone in office, especially those who’ve been in office for decades. Party leaders have been forced to embrace leftist candidates in some instances, and I think that trend will continue – these candidates often come with popularity in their districts or cities, and they have online audiences that party leaders will want to capitalize on. They’ll also need them, depending on how many there are, to maintain their leadership roles, though I think there are growing voices who want to see both Schumer and Jeffries replaced. There’s been a lot of talk about truly making the party a “big tent,” but a lot of work needed to make that a reality. And I will note, too, that while the right brought the Tea Party in, and then Maga in, it has basically excommunicated moderate Republicans in recent years. Moderate Republicans get ousted in their primaries almost as a rule now. Lauramax100 asks: Could being too united be a bad thing? It was a real turn-off when party elders tried so hard to interfere in the NYC mayoral election even after primary voters made their choice. Could celebrating a broad coalition and letting local people choose be a better approach? The Republicans weren’t totally united pre-Trump, and arguably his attempt to have an iron grip on all GOP politicians may be one part of that party’s undoing. Joseph: Unity can easily tip into groupthink, and the reluctance of leaders like Schumer and Jeffries to back Mamdani after he clearly (resoundingly?) won the primary looked to many like exactly that … the elite and old guard second-guessing where the voters have moved, which is why even allies like AOC called it a bad look. Trump’s “iron grip” model has won elections, but I’d argue it’s brittle: it depends on near-total deference to one man, punishes dissent that might otherwise catch mistakes early, and leaves the party with little to correct course once he’s gone. The Democrats’ instinct to litigate every nominee’s ideological purity risks the opposite type of failure. It’s a party so busy relitigating primaries that it struggles to actually fight the other side. They must come to terms with what the voters are not asking for, but now demanding of their elected officials. David: I agree with Joseph that the Trump cult is brittle: like an authoritarian regime, investing so much in one leader means a lack of flexibility and diversity of thought. And, like an authoritarian regime, Republicans will now have to wrestle with the succession question of who comes next. Democrats holding feisty debates of ideas is a healthier way to go. But as we’ve seen, especially in the social media era, that can easily become corrosive and turn into a circular firing squad. Some have observed that Democratic moderates are more venomous towards progressives than they are towards Republicans! They have to get the balance right and unite around their nominee in 2028. nycreader2 asks: Abdul El-Sayed has become a major symbol of the debate over the party’s direction. Are there other races or candidates we should be watching if we want to understand where Democrats are heading? Rachel Leingang: There are so many interesting races this year – and I don’t think there will be one clean narrative about who wins. El-Sayed’s race remains one of the most interesting, though Democrats (and a couple independents) in typically redder places could win running economic populist campaigns that largely avoid cultural issues, and there will likely be more progressives in Congress based on who won the primaries. I’m based in the Midwest, so I’m paying close attention to: – David Crowley vs Tom Tiffany in the Wisconsin governor’s race – Rebecca Cooke’s third attempt to unseat Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s third congressional district – Basically every federal and statewide race in Iowa: Rob Sand for governor, Josh Turek for Senate, three of the four congressional races – Dan Osborn’s run as an independent for US Senate in Nebraska, as well as a couple congressional campaigns there – Adam Hamilton, a Democratic pastor, is making a case he could win in Kansas – Sherrod Brown’s attempt to return to the US Senate in Ohio, along with a few congressional races there that could flip seats – In Michigan, Will Lawrence’s progressive campaign in a split district Shrai Popat: Just to piggyback off Rachel here, a few that I’ve been covering and fascinated by across the country: – Troy Jackson in Maine. He’s the replacement Democratic nominee after the truly wild primary race blew up when Graham Platner was accused of sexual assault (which he denies) and ended his campaign. Jackson, who is a logger and former state lawmaker, is trying to unseat Susan Collins – a moderate Republican who is hoping to secure a sixth term in office. – Chris Pappas in New Hampshire. He’s a moderate congressman who has kept his once purple district blue. He’s hoping to keep the open Senate seat in Democratic control, but facing a tough contest against John E Sununu – a former senator from a political dynasty who has been comfortable criticizing Trump in the past (even though he bagged the president’s endorsement this cycle). Notably, Pappas beat his progressive challenger in the primary. New Hampshire really is emblematic of what a purple state looks like. Fully Democratic congressional delegation but Republican control of the legislature. Harris won in 2024, but the state still elected a GOP governor. What’s interesting to me in both of these New England Senate races is how Trump’s support could easily be an albatross for both of these Republicans as opposed to an asset. They’ll have to navigate unpopular opinions about the administration among moderates/swing voters, but also satisfy the Maga base. Another race that continues to be a prime example of picking a Democratic nominee with huge momentum is the Texas Senate race. Here, James Talarico, a polished state lawmaker, is facing a Trump loyalist – Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Talarico has touted his religious beliefs, and walked back some of his more socially progressive comments. He’s also praised the incumbent senator John Cornyn, who lost the GOP primary to Paxton this year. NorthLondonIsRed asks: Since Zohran Mamdani’s election as NYC Mayor some Democratic leaders (Schumer, Jeffries) have kept their distance from him and the DSA, while others (Hochul, Harris, AOC, Sanders) have pushed for unity. As the party’s left wing gains national visibility ahead of the 2026 midterms will Democrats consolidate the way the GOP did under Trump — or will the centrist/progressive divide deepen into a functional three-party split? David Smith says: I think they’ll be fine before the midterms. They will have progressives running in some districts and moderates in others, with anti-Trump sentiment as the glue holding them together. One exception might be Michigan, where many Democrats have got on board with progressive Abdul El-Sayed but some have not. After the midterms, however, there is potential for a split. If El-Sayed loses, there will be lots of finger pointing and claims that a progressive can’t win in 2028. But if El-Sayed and democratic socialists do well, it could be game on for Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 2028. Alice Speri: I don’t think this is going to be as much of an issue in the midterms. I think even Democrats who are unhappy about the DSA wins will prioritize defeating Republicans. I do think these tensions will be dominating the presidential primaries though and many are already gearing up for that. Third Way, a centrist Democratic group, announced a $15m effort to go to “war” against DSA. I don’t think that whatever unity Democrats manage to find in November will last. We’re less than two months from the midterm elections that could have an outsized impact on the future of the United States. With the primaries wrapped, our reporting team is fanned out across the country to tell the stories behind the horse race, from Washington to the Midwest and along the West Coast. One of the key questions is, with the Democrats poised to take the House and perhaps even the Senate, what the rise of the party’s progressive left means for the broader Democrat coalition. How will candidates such as Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed co-exist with the party’s more established centrists – and will the growing influence of democratic socialists push the party in a new direction? Political breaking news correspondent Joseph Gedeon, Midwest political correspondent, Rachel Leingang, US politics live blogger Shrai Popat; Washington bureau chief David Smith and reporter, Alice Speri are here live answering your questions. Sign up or sign in to join the discussion.

webTitle: More Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into view

fields.headline: More Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into view
fields.trailText: Three more GOP members voted for war powers resolution to force withdrawal from the conflict as election looms
fields.bodyText: As the US war with Iran drags on, the ranks of Republicans signaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow. When the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trump proposed impeaching the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization. The rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. But they underscore the growing nerves among both the party’s most vulnerable and most disobedient lawmakers over continuing a conflict that appears to have accomplished little other than play into the hands of Democrats, who have spent the entirety of Trump’s second term arguing that only they can be trusted to lower costs for Americans. “I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” said the congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, one of the trio of Republicans who for the first time supported a war powers resolution. She was joined by another Iowa Republican, Zach Nunn, who justified his vote by noting his state “has already paid a devastating price” in the conflict, with two Iowans among the US soldiers killed by Iranian attacks as the war began. “Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” the congressman said. “Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.” Since the US joined Israel in attacking Iran at the end of February, Democrats have wielded war powers resolutions as a cudgel to get Republicans on the record about a conflict that polls indicate is not popular with the public. Their first three attempts failed, but in June, the fourth passed with the votes of two libertarian-minded Republicans – Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio – along with Tom Barrett of Michigan and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom occupy battlefield districts. The Senate later approved that measure, but Trump refused to abide by it. In July, the same lineup in the House passed a fifth war powers resolution, before Nunn, Miller-Meeks and Nancy Mace of South Carolina expanded the ranks of Republican objectors to seven in Tuesday’s vote. The two Iowans are among the Republicans considered most at risk of losing re-election in the November midterms, with Miller-Meeks having won her race two years ago by fewer than 800 votes. They also represent areas of a state where the market impacts of the war with Iran are pronounced, as Iowa farmers struggle with higher prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer, all of which have been compounded by Trump’s tariff regime. Iowa has drifted consistently to the right over the past decade, but this year, Democrats believe the circumstances are right for them to oust not just Miller-Meeks and Nunn, but also to win a Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and potentially more congressional districts in the state. It’s far from the only state where Democrats are on the offensive. The House vote took place on the same day the New York Times and Siena University released polling that showed likely voters preferred Democrats over Republicans for Congress by nearly nine percentage point, a finding that lines up with other surveys. Democrats are helped in their quest to retake the House by the fact that Republicans control it with a tiny majority that may be exceedingly hard to defend in November, and has also enabled Republicans like Massie to seize on splits within the party to embarrass Trump and his ally the House speaker, Mike Johnson. Last year, Massie banded together with Democrats and a handful of Republican dissidents to force passage of a bill requiring the release of files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein. That intensified the president’s ire towards him, and Massie lost his primary to the Trump-endorsed Republican Ed Gallrein earlier this year. Now with even less to lose, the congressman appears to be trying to seize on splits within the House GOP to retaliate against Hegseth, who campaigned for Gallrein. Massie proposed the resolution on Tuesday, and House rules appear to require it be voted on by Thursday. The chamber was scheduled to be in session that day for the last time before the 3 November midterm elections, but on Wednesday morning, House Republican leaders canceled votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home early to face their constituents.

webTitle: House speaker calls early recess before midterms amid AI regulation frenzy

fields.headline: House speaker calls early recess before midterms amid AI regulation frenzy
fields.trailText: Mike Johnson cancels votes on Thursday, meaning House members will avoid voting on impeaching Pete Hegseth
fields.bodyText: The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. It’s the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday. “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump. “We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. “Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.” More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards. In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place on Wednesday afternoon. A spokesperson for Johnson characterized the House speaker’s latest move as simply moving up scheduled votes, not canceling future votes. Speaking to reporters outside of his office on Wednesday, Johnson said he was modifying the schedule because “the House has done its work”. Johnson said he wanted members to return to their districts to spend time with constituents ahead of the election. “You’ve seen the statistics we’ve been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789,” Johnson said, repeating a claim he also made earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention. However, so far, the current session has fallen short of passing legislation to surpass the two previous House sessions, according to the fact-checking website Snopes. Johnson also addressed Massie’s impeachment resolution, calling it “a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention”. The House speaker insisted it would be “immediately” postponed and he would not address it before the recess because the US is in the middle of international conflicts. Lawmakers will likely face a busy legislative agenda when they return to Capitol Hill after election day in November. Among their priorities will be addressing Massie’s resolution on impeaching Hegseth because it was filed as privileged, which fast-tracks the resolution.

webTitle: How Jon Ossoff won the algorithm – and garnered Obama comparisons ahead of 2028

fields.headline: How Jon Ossoff won the algorithm – and garnered Obama comparisons ahead of 2028
fields.trailText: Pictures of Georgia Democrat looking into middle distance proliferate – and social media skills have boosted his profile
fields.bodyText: Delivering a speech in Atlanta last month, Jon Ossoff accused Donald Trump of corruption, incompetence and fecklessness, and peppered his remarks with substantive observations of dates and times and places. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One. The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall. After his remark went viral, stories about Trump’s young, exceptionally devoted, presidential aide Natalie Harp rippled through social and established media. Often enough, they were accompanied by an image of Ossoff, his sharp jawline captured from below as he looks into the middle distance. This photographic framing has increasingly been referred to as the “Ossoff angle”, perhaps in a disservice to myriad politicians from John F Kennedy to Barack Obama who also employed the technique, snapped at a low angle from a camera pit over the past century. While the approach is not new, it has helped the senator for Georgia to reach the social media feeds of users far beyond his state. Kathleen Hall Jamieson, professor of communication at Penn’s Annenberg School, likened Ossoff to Kennedy. The first millennial senator has mastered the medium of the moment, she suggested, much as Kennedy was the first president who really understood television. “How do you communicate that this is a new generation of leadership?,” Jamieson asked. “And how do you do that rhetorically? Because you can’t just stand up and say, ‘This is a new generation of leadership.’ “You have to have people draw that conclusion about you. And part of the way you do that is you master the media of the time, and you demonstrate that in the process you have leadership capacity and that you have the capacity to deal with the old order.” At 33 years, 11 months and four days, Ossoff was the youngest US senator sworn into the 117th Congress. At 39 today, and ever so slightly gray at the temple, he remains the youngest in a chamber with an average age of 65. The value of good lighting, a good background and a good angle in a social media post is not lost on a film-maker, as Ossoff was before turning to public office. The former documentarian has a knack for winning the algorithm with plain language, surfacing absurdities in an era of absurdities. While Trump is also a master of social media, the effect is different. His audience is generationally different. Trump, who regularly attaches infantile nicknames to his political enemies as a political marketing gimmick, calls Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman”, a tepid sobriquet which hasn’t yet landed. More recently, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned Super Pac, began running ads about Ossoff’s haircare and makeup regime using AI-generated videos of Ossoff in a salon chair. (Ossoff has spent about $1,200 on hair and makeup this election cycle – a drop in the bucket, given a fundraising haul of $81m up to June, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) disclosures.) Georgia elected Ossoff in a nail-biting runoff in January 2021 with control of the Senate on the line, amid the turmoil of Trump’s election dispute. His election, alongside fellow Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock, secured the Senate majority for Democrats. Rioters stormed the US Capitol the next day. Since taking office, Ossoff has built a high profile as an opponent of Washington corruption, maladministration and the so-called Epstein class. He grilled CIA director John Ratcliffe after Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, published a report that senior officials had shared sensitive information about future military strikes on Signal with him. He pressed Russ Vought, Trump’s budget director, after massive cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He questioned former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard on her presence at an FBI raid that seized 2020 ballots in Fulton county. His questioning of such Trump administration officials have proven as likely to reach wide social media audiences as anything he says on the campaign trail. Clips circulated of Ossoff repeatedly pressing intelligence director nominee Jay Clayton during a July 2026 hearing to say plainly whether the 2020 election was legitimate. Ossoff’s questions left Clayton sitting in silence at the hearing table, refusing to speak. “Your answers lack credibility,” Ossoff declared. “Your testimony lacks credibility. You’re being evasive and you’re not being candid or forthright. And everybody across the country is going to watch this and know that.” But outside of the spotlight, Ossoff has held hearings on child welfare and federal prison abuses both in Washington DC and across the state of Georgia. These relatively quiet issues tend to draw little media attention and less financial interest from funders, though they are a vital element of government oversight. “It is clear that Jon Ossoff believes what he is saying, and people – they get it,” said Charlie Bailey, chairman of Georgia’s Democratic party. “And so it not only matches up with their experience and their their anger and their frustration, they know he’s telling the truth. They know he’s saying what he believes, and that’s why he’s saying it, because he thinks it’s the right thing to do.”
